Though we assume lower prices we remain positive on commodities as a whole with higher precious and base metals to 2012, our preference in the medium term is for copper, PGMs and thermal coal. We have also adjusted our short term ZARUS$ weaker. The result is generally lower earnings and NPVs. ###### **Retaining our bullish commodity view, prefer precious/traded commodities** Market concerns are turning to the possibility that current events may precipitate a similar crisis to the one that unfolded in 2008. Naturally if this were to occur it would have negative implications for commodity markets. However, we believe that 1

) financial market leverage is smaller, 2) liquidity backstops are present in the form of unlimited support by the ECB and 3) investors are better able to manage counterparty and liquidity risk. As a result, we remain overweight precious metals and traded commodities and have a relatively more bearish view on the bulks. ###### **We continue to prefer Anglo over BHP** We continue to prefer Anglo over BHP. We think Anglo has further value to be realised from delivery of growth and de-gearing leading to special dividends and further growth project approvals. BHP offers value as a defensive exposure and ZAR/US$ hedge among the general miners with a similarly attractive valuation. ###### **Among the mid caps we favour ARM and Exxaro** _This report changes ratings, price targets, and estimates for several companies under coverage. Individual analyst contributions have been_ Is it different this time?** **_noted at the end of each section._** - - Market concerns are turning to the possibility that events today may precipitate a similar crisis to the one that unfolded in 2008. Naturally if this were to occur it would have negative implications for commodity markets. - However, we believe that there are three important differences between now and three years ago. First, financial market leverage is smaller, whether measured through positioning in various asset classes or the size of bank assets relative to capital. - Second, liquidity backstops are present in the form of unlimited MRO/TRO operations by the ECB under looser collateral rules, swap lines between the Fed and other central banks, and an accumulated pool of US$ liquidity as a result of the Fed's QE operations. - Third, investors are better prepared; with a shift to collateralized borrowing and bigger pools of accumulated liquidity meaning market participants are better able to manage counterparty and liquidity risk. - As a result, we are unlikely to experience a simultaneous and large-scale unwind of positions of the scale seen in 2008. This difference has been evident over the last few months, with the crisis first hitting European sovereign bond markets (July), then shifting to European credit and equity markets (August), and now spilling over to EM assets. There is therefore a marked contrast between the disjointed nature of the risk

unwind today compared to the simultaneous sell-off in September 2008. - The second difference is that the negative feedback loops are likely to take much longer to materialize and spread outside of Europe. In 2008, the main element of contagion from the US to the global economy was through the simultaneous collapse in asset prices as well as a freezing up in trade credit. The former hit global demand, while the latter saw a collapse in global trade volumes. Both hit economic growth. - This time round, the decline in global asset prices is smaller due to lower leverage, and trade credit has not frozen, implying that any spill-over of the European financial crisis to the rest of the world is more likely to take place through macroeconomic, rather than financial channels. **_Michael Lewis, (44) 20 7545 2166_** _michael.lewis@db.com_ ###### **_George Saravelos, (44) 20 7547 9118_** _george.saravelos@db.com_ Deutsche Securities (Pty) Ltd Page 8 27 September 2011 General Mining SA General Mining ###### **_This table is an extract from_** The following table summarises our key macro forecasts: |**_the ‘Global Economic_**

We believe this is noteworthy since it not only suggests that the price rally over the past decade has been relatively orderly, but that in the event of further market dislocation gold price gains could accelerate on a par with the 1970s. - However, the latest correction in the gold price to under US$1,700/oz has raised concerns that the bubble has burst. Indeed events today appear reminiscent of the silver price correction in the second quarter of this year not least since both corrections occurred soon after margin requirement on the CME were increased. - Another worrying development has been the negative correlation between the US do

llar and the gold price reasserting itself. We believe this reflects the moderation in inflows into physically backed gold ETFs during periods of risk aversion over the past three years, a sign perhaps that investor holdings are close to saturation point. 

- However, the commitment by the US Federal Reserve to keep interest rates on hold for the next two years and no apparent resolution to the European banking crisis mean that we are leaving our bullish gold price forecasts into 2012, published in the Commodities Quarterly in July, unchanged. 

- We continue to view the development of a bubble across parts of the precious metals complex as a high probability event over the coming year. On our estimates, overvaluation in gold starts to appear above US$2,175/oz. 

- Even in the absence of extreme financial market contagion, history would suggest that the current level of US real interest rates would be indicative of gold and silver returns respectively averaging 40% and 20% per annum. 

- Over the past decade investor demand has risen from less than 10% of total demand to approximately 45% today. This represents the largest share of financial sector activity in any commodity market. 

- We find that physically backed gold ETFs have become an efficient vehicle to gain exposure to gold not least because there has been a significant under-performance in the equity of gold producing companies relative to gold ETFs since the onset of the financial crisis in 2007.

#### **Platinum Group Metals** 

- The outlook for the PGM complex has deteriorated over the past three months. The repercussions for a Greek default, be it orderly or not, is clearly a bad outcome for European auto demand and by consequence the platinum demand centre. 

- Similarly slowing economic activity in China and weaker than expected growth in the US have dampened the demand outlook for palladium. 

- Operating conditions in South Africa remain challenging, and we believe there are still downside risks to supply forecasts for the PGMs. 

- The combination of weaker demand and much more modest growth expectations, albeit with downside risks, should see the platinum market remain in a fundamental surplus until 2013F.

#### **Industrial Metals** 

- Alongside energy, industrial metal prices have typically been most vulnerable in periods of extreme financial market dislocation. In this section, we examine potential downside risks for the complex in the current environment of risk aversion. 

- While China represents the lion’s share of metals demand growth, the EU and the US account f

or a significant portion of global consumption. In our view, a downturn in the EU and the US could hurt nickel demand the most due to its higher usage in the region. 

- Cross-asset correlation between industrial metals, equity markets and EURUS$ has increased during the latest bout of risk aversion. On our analysis, nickel is most exposed to equity market weakness while aluminium has been more resilient to equity market sell-offs. 

- Despite aggressive liquidation over the past two months, we find that the copper price is still trading at a significant premium over marginal cost of production. If deflationary forces intensify, this premium could fall to 80% in our view, which would be indicative of copper prices around US$6,600/tonne. 

- In terms of long term fair value, we examine long run marginal cost , incentive pricing as well as the average of historical prices. We find that aluminium and zinc are trading at a discount to their long term fair value suggesting potential downside support on this basis. 

- As financial markets price in a global recession , we also examined metals demand destruction during four recessionary periods: 1980, 1981-82, 1990-91, 2001. We found that industrial metals demand typically declined by 3-4% during mild recessions. We then compare market balances in our base case scenario and a recessionary scenario. 

- On a relative value basis, we favour aluminium in a deflationary environment . Our analysis shows that aluminium typically outperforms during US/EU recessions.

#### **Crude Oil** 

- Three factors are keeping the oil markets on the defensive : (1) economic worries driven by the US budget debate and the European debt crisis, (2) the potential return of Libyan oil exports, and (3) financial factors- including weaker US equity markets and a possibly stronger dollar. The cumulative effect of these issues, we believe, is acting to keep oil prices range-bound over the next year. 

- Deutsche Bank’s forecasts for world GDP growth have been trimmed again and we now expect global growth of 3.7% in 2012. We continue to characterize the outlook as a “slowdown”, not a “recession” , but believe that downside risks are accumulating. 

- After an astounding 2.7mmb/d gain in 2010, the consensus for 2011 oil demand growth is drifting toward a rise of 1.2mmb/d. As GDP estimates are adjusted (likely downward) for 2012, oil demand forecasts cuts are probable. 

- Non-OPEC supply growth forecasts for 2012 may have upside potential. Global oil prices have remained robust and technological improvements are boosting recovery rates, especially in the US. 

- Although OPEC NGL production growth is starting to slow down, growth in 2012 looks likely to average near 0.4 mmb/d. This output, in conjunction with non-OPEC liquids, is enough to meet demand. 

- Our forecasts for th

e total “call on OPEC crude” in 2012 allows for some growth in OPEC output as global inventories need rebuilding. - OECD company-controlled inventories in July fell below the five-year average for the first time since 2008. The IEA says that stocks remain “tight” in August, and we suspect this situation will continue. This helps explain the backwardation in the Brent forward curve. - OPEC spare capacity is likely to improve as the recovery in Libyan exports gets underway, but we believe this will be a protracted process. - We expect Brent crude to average US$115/bbl, with WTI at US$95/bbl. The WTI-Brent spread should narrow as transportation bottlenecks out of Cushing are reduced. Our forecast for Brent to reach US$125/bbl in 2015 remains unchanged. ###### **_Adam Sieminski, (1) 202 662 1624_** _adam.sieminski@db.com_ Deutsche Securities (Pty) Ltd Page 13 27 September 2011 General Mining SA General Mining # **3Q11 review** #### **Methodology** In this section, the 3Q11 performance of companies, commodities and currencies have been compared to quarterly historical performance (from 2Q00). Recent news is better for Minas Rio with construction now well underway and the pipeline and port ahead of the critical path schedule. 

We also expect Anglo to continue to progress on the sales of non-core assets over the next 6-12 months. The divestment of Scaw South Africa is expected in 2H11 and Tarmac will follow in the next 18-24 months in our view. 

Anglo management is now focused on growth and we expect more information on a number of growth projects in the next year. We have found that Anglo has inferior longer term growth without replacement projects and thus that the upcoming project approvals expected are likely to match Anglo’s growth path to peers rather than be a differentiating factor. 

Taking Anglo’s growth spurt (12.3% copper equivalent CAGR growth from 2011-2013) into account at the same time as the end of capex for the four major growth projects we see a window of free cash flow generation leading to industry differentiated special dividends. Our analysis highlights the potential for US$10bn of special dividends in the next three years. The greatest risk to this view is the potential for M&A, an area where Anglo has confirmed their interest but to date has been disciplined and has not executed in the recent high price deal environment. 

Our price target reflects a valuation taking into consideration both DCF over life-of-mine (9.5% WACC - Beta 1.25, ERP 4.5%, Rf 5%, COD 6% on a through-the-cycle target gearing of 30%) for core asset valuations and market values or peer group multiples for non-core assets. We value at 1x NPV in line with its long-term average and what we believe is the market's unwillingness to pay for more than approved growth. Risks to our view include stronger-than-expected operating currencies (Rand, A$) and lower commodity prices, in particular PGMs, copper and iron ore. More specific risks include lack of delivery on asset optimisation, procurement targets as well as non-core asset sales and the turnaround of AngloPlat and De Beers.
